extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, legal scholars, judges, and policymakers working on AI, tort, consumer-protection, and defamation law
extracted.subtask_description: Scholarly analysis of how existing legal doctrines (defamation, negligence, products liability, res ipsa loquitur, consumer protection) apply to harms and deceptive practices involving AI, and why technology-specific legislation is often counterproductive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defamation — origin irrelevant; duty to correct on knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors in what a company communicates can be defamatory regardless of whether the errors stem from direct human error in composing text or from human error in creating the technology that produces the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existing defamation principles govern even LLM-generated statements because liability turns on a human actor’s design error or knowledge and continued publication rather than the statement’s origin. A publisher who learns its own statement is false and defamatory has a duty to remove or correct it; continued publication after notice can give rise to liability (likened to keeping graffiti displayed after learning of it).

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability for continued publication after notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Liability will arise where the LLM’s design is not defective, but where the LLM creator is made aware of the defamatory content but nonetheless continues to publish it despite an opportunity to correct the error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Awareness of false or defamatory output plus continued publication can create publisher-like liability; remedial duty to remove or correct once put on notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Products liability — defect categories (Restatement Third §2)
rubrics_metrics.description: A product is defective when, at the time of sale or distribution, it contains a manufacturing defect, is defective in design, or is defective because of inadequate instructions or warnings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard products-liability framework applies to AI-driven products (self-driving cars, medical devices, etc.). Manufacturers bear responsibility for defects; users for harms caused by negligent use; courts/juries evaluate reasonableness under the circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negligence framework for semiautonomous systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Accidents traceable to error by human drivers of semiautonomous vehicles are well-governed under standard negligence law (general duty of reasonable care).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where harm can be attributed to a human act or omission, negligence doctrine assigns responsibility. The Restatement principles regarding duty and reasonableness govern inquiries into operator conduct and oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution difficulty — limits of fault-based regimes
rubrics_metrics.description: Some machine behaviors may defy easy attribution of fault either to operator or manufacturer, particularly where no single design flaw or programming misstep can be pinpointed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opaque, black-box chains of perception/action (misclassification, sensor errors, complex subsystem interactions) strain negligence and design-defect frameworks because causation cannot easily be traced to discrete human decisions. These factual unfamiliarities require adaptation within existing doctrines rather than wholesale replacement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Option to retain negligence (no-fault absence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not every person who suffers an accident is entitled to a compensatory legal award; only those injured by another’s wrongful conduct. If an injured party has not been wronged or cannot prove she has been wronged, there is no legal basis for recovery from a third party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintaining negligence preserves fault-based limitations on recovery; private insurance is an efficient alternative to address losses that fall outside fault-based recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict products liability as a tool for AI-caused physical injury
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the mid-twentieth century, tort law has accommodated plaintiffs’ difficulty proving manufacturers’ negligence by adopting a strict products liability regime that reduces or eliminates the burden to prove negligence where a plaintiff is injured by a defective product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strict liability (especially for manufacturing defects) imposes liability without proof of fault and has been proposed as a response to inscrutable AI-caused harms. However, in practice strict doctrine has drifted toward negligence for design and warning defects, often requiring proof of a reasonable alternative design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Res ipsa loquitur for opaque causation cases
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of res ipsa loquitur presumes the defendant’s carelessness and shifts the burden of proof to the defendant to show that she acted with adequate care if the accident is the sort of thing that ordinarily happens only as a result of negligence by someone in the defendant’s position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Res ipsa has practical use in products liability involving automated features where direct evidence of causation is difficult (e.g., sudden unintended acceleration litigation). It functions as a burden-shifting tool when circumstantial evidence supports an inference of manufacturer responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hybrid negligence standard (compare AI to humans and algorithms)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed hybrid negligence standard would gauge the reasonableness of AI performance in comparison to both humans and other algorithms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under Diamantis’s approach, 'an AI engaged in some task is reasonable if it causes less harm than the weighted average of harm that all actors—both AI and human—cause while engaged in that task.' This preserves fault-based structure while updating the comparator class to reflect AI’s nonhuman character; it is one among multiple viable adaptations.

rubrics_metrics.name: No single correct legal solution — multiple workable schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: Many legal approaches could work (retain negligence, adopt strict liability, use res ipsa, adopt hybrid standards); there may be a role for several schemes depending on context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law’s basic structure is resilient and offers a menu of possible approaches; the choice among them depends on context-specific tradeoffs rather than the need for entirely new foundational doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer protection — dark patterns fall within existing law
rubrics_metrics.description: Dark patterns—interfaces that pressure or manipulate users—fall squarely within long-standing consumer protection law, including common-law fraud, the FTC Act, and state consumer protection statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The legal response depends on the substance of the conduct (misrepresentation, deception), not the digital method. Misleading user interfaces can be policed under fraud doctrines and statutory provisions that prohibit 'unfair or deceptive acts or practices.'

rubrics_metrics.name: FTC/Section 5 standard — 'likely to mislead' reasonable consumer
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 5 of the FTC Act and analogous state laws declare unlawful all 'unfair or deceptive acts or practices,' which the FTC has long interpreted to prohibit any representation 'likely to mislead the consumer acting reasonably in the circumstances.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory consumer-protection enforcement often eliminates the need to prove fraudulent intent; the operative inquiry is likelihood to mislead a reasonable consumer. The FTC has used this authority to challenge harmful dark patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Range of dark-pattern severity and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Dark patterns range from mild (preselected email opt-in, promotional warnings) to aggressive/deceptive (fake countdown timers, fabricated scarcity alerts, hidden prechecked boxes, intentionally confusing double negatives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milder tactics may be annoyances consumers can avoid; more deceptive tactics distort choice architecture and produce inefficient market outcomes (subscribe/consent/regret). Legal scrutiny focuses on misleading or materially deceptive practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance-over-tech principle — focus on conduct, not tool
rubrics_metrics.description: The law’s response to dark patterns, like their low‑tech forebears, depends on the substance of the defendant’s conduct, not the method of deceptive communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existing doctrines (fraud, FTC Act, state UDAP statutes) cover misleading design practices; new technology-specific laws are unnecessary to reach the harmful practices in most cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid technology-specific lawmaking — particularization harms
rubrics_metrics.description: Particularized statutes tailored to novel technologies typically add complexity without adding clarity, raise compliance costs by layering new obligations atop existing ones, generate inconsistencies by regulating one technological path while leaving nearly identical conduct via other means untouched, and open the door to reconsideration of foundational legal principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technology-specific law risks ossification (becoming relics), regulatory overlap, increased costs, and political capture; lawmakers should prefer general rules that adapt across contexts unless there is a compelling reason otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hayekian knowledge problem — limits on legislating AI
rubrics_metrics.description: Lawmakers do not, and cannot, know enough to legislate wisely in fast-changing environments because the knowledge required is dispersed, tacit, localized, and often unarticulated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective regulation would require granular technical knowledge (sensor capabilities, algorithms) and localized information (community traffic norms, infrastructure idiosyncrasies), which cannot be centralized without risking regulatory capture and error. This epistemic constraint counsels humility and caution about bespoke AI statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of legal generality and incremental adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: The law’s strength lies in its generality: common-law principles endure because they are flexible and apply across contexts, technologies, and generations, adapting to new facts without requiring wholesale reinvention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generality provides predictability that encourages investment and innovation; ad hoc, technology-specific rules often age poorly and destabilize settled legal norms.
